title: Carbon tax

definition.text: A carbon tax is a tax charged on the carbon released when goods and services are produced.

facts.text: It aims to make the hidden social costs of carbon emissions visible by raising the price of fossil fuels.
Higher prices cut demand for high-emission goods and push producers to make them less carbon-intensive.
Unlike command-and-control rules that cap each polluter, a carbon tax lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution.
Its design turns on two choices: how high to set the tax, usually based on the social cost of carbon, and what to do with the revenue.
In its simplest form it covers only CO2, but it can also tax methane or nitrous oxide by their CO2-equivalent warming potential.
Research shows carbon taxes do often reduce emissions; a 2015 British Columbia study found cuts of 5–15% with negligible overall economic effects.
As of 2019 carbon taxes had been implemented or scheduled in 25 countries, and 46 countries priced carbon in some form.
David Gordon Wilson first proposed this type of tax in 1973.

contested_note: Studies find it can hit poor households harder than rich ones, but Gilbert Metcalf disputed that it would be regressive in the US.

title: Carbon leakage

definition.text: Carbon leakage is the rise in greenhouse gas emissions in one country that results from emission cuts in another country with stricter climate policy.

facts.text: It happens when regulating emissions in one place pushes them to places with less regulation.
If climate policy raises local costs, production may move to a country with laxer rules and global emissions are not reduced.
It is measured as the rise in emissions outside the acting countries divided by the cut inside them, as a percentage that can exceed 100%.
Leakage can also run the good way: lower fossil fuel demand in rich countries may cut prices and let poorer countries swap coal for oil or gas.
There is no consensus on how large long-term leakage effects are.

contested_note: Sources say there is no consensus over the magnitude of long-term leakage.

definition.text: A carbon tariff, or border carbon adjustment, is a charge on imports according to the carbon emitted in making them.

facts.text: Its usual aim is to prevent carbon leakage from states that have no carbon price.
High-carbon imports that might face one include coal-fired electricity, blast-furnace iron and steel, and fertilizer from the Haber process.
Only California applies one for electricity, while the European Union and the United Kingdom will apply them from 2026 and 2027.
Carbon credits, carbon taxes and Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms are all forms of carbon pricing.

title: Environmental tax

definition.text: An environmental tax, also called an ecotax or green tax, is a tax on activities that harm the environment, meant to steer people toward cleaner alternatives.

facts.text: Ecotaxes are a kind of Pigouvian tax, a tax on goods whose making or use imposes costs on others.
They can address the failure of free markets to limit environmental harm, and can complement or replace command-and-control regulation.
Ireland's €0.22 plastic bag tax cut plastic bags' share of litter from 5% to 0.13% in 14 years and raised over €200 million.
Because the poor spend more of their income on consumption, taxes on consumption can be regressive.
Germany enacted an ecotax through laws in 1998, 1999 and 2002, cutting income taxes so the total tax burden stayed constant.
In 2018 China replaced its 1979 Pollutant Discharge Fee with an environmental protection tax.
Economists critical of degrowth argue that price incentives through environmental taxes or tradable permits are much more effective.

contested_note: Some green tax shift proposals have been criticized as regressive, falling harder on poorer households.

definition.text: Environmental taxes are usually sorted into four categories: energy, transport, pollution and resource taxes.

facts.text: Energy taxes, levied on producing, distributing or using fuels such as coal, oil and gas, are the most common environmental taxes worldwide.
Transport taxes, the second most notable kind, fall on vehicle ownership and use, such as registration taxes based on weight, fuel efficiency or emissions.
Pollution taxes cover measured emissions to air and water and the management of waste and noise.
Resource taxes on extracting water, forests or wildlife are the least common; depletion is usually handled by government fees instead.

definition.text: An emissions tax makes each emitter pay a charge for every tonne of greenhouse gas it releases, while an energy tax is charged on the fuels themselves.

facts.text: Emissions taxes and energy taxes are two taxes closely related to the carbon tax.
A carbon tax encourages using less fuel but does not reward cutting emissions by other means such as carbon capture and storage, so it is not a perfect substitute for an emissions tax.
